questions.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}-6 & -6 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=0,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}r(-4t)={e}^{-4t} \\ r(0)=1\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{0}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{0}=1.
$$

- Substituting ${\alpha }_{0}=1$ into the first equation, we get

$$
-4t{\alpha }_{1}+1={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-1).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-6(-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-1))t+1 \\  & =\frac{6}{4}({e}^{-4t}-1)+1 \\  & =\frac{3}{2}({e}^{-4t}-1)+1 \\  & =\frac{-3+3{e}^{-4t}+2}{2} \\  & =\frac{-1+3{e}^{-4t}}{2} \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2(-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-1))t \\  & =-\frac{2}{4}({e}^{-4t}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-4t}-1) \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-4t}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1+3{e}^{-4t} & -3+3{e}^{-4t} \\ 1-{e}^{-4t} & 3-{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}].
$$

- Multiplying the first equation by $4$ and subtracting the second one, we get

$$
3\alpha_0 = 4e^{t} - e^{4t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_0 = \dfrac{1}{3}\bigl(4e^{t}-e^{4t}\bigr).
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t}))t+\frac{1}{3}(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t}+4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}) \\  & ={e}^{t} \\ -3{\alpha }_{1}t & =-3(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t}))t \\  & ={e}^{t}-{e}^{4t} \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4(\frac{1}{3t}({e}^{4t}-{e}^{t}))t+\frac{1}{3}(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}((4{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{t})+(4{e}^{t}-{e}^{4t})) \\  & ={e}^{4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix Exponent for a Matrix With Distinct Complex Eigenvalues
canonical_examples.problem:
Find $e^{At}$ for ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14058518/assets/3f97cbbd4715d8191dc5b0c410a784b556b068ed5e3e57fe0dc16ee8f52655cc.png) 

*Hint: The eigenvalues of $A$ are $3 \pm 2\textrm{i}.$*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ -5 & -1\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 4{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues or $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1= (3+2\textrm{i}) t, \qquad
\lambda_2= (3-2\textrm{i}) t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((3+2\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(3+2\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(3+2\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & ={e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\ (3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0})+2{\alpha }_{1}\text{i}t & ={e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\,{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}3{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}={e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =\frac{7}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)), \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t & =4\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t \\  & =2{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & =-5\cdot \frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t), \\ -{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-\frac{1}{2t}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t+{e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+{e}^{3t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{3t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & ={e}^{3t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

canonical_examples.problem:
Find $e^{At}$ for ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14058518/assets/9657b1346f9aa79eaa2d05d0a94b5e13745fedc83b035cbd59f1efdb10ce19bf.png) 

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $6,$ and it has multiplicity two.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
\lambda_1 = 6t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}r(6t)={e}^{6t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
\alpha_1 = e^{6t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
6t e^{6t} + \alpha_0 = e^{6t}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\alpha_0 = e^{6t}(1-6t).
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the required entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =8{e}^{6t}t+{e}^{6t}(1-6t) \\  & ={e}^{6t}(1+2t), \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & =-2{e}^{6t}t \\  & ={e}^{6t}(-2t), \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2{e}^{6t}t \\  & ={e}^{6t}(2t), \\ 4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4{e}^{6t}t+{e}^{6t}(1-6t) \\  & ={e}^{6t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14058518/assets/f97a3d1392b000bb1f02f0f8cd567b72d1a6792e4bc9da41ea24cc4ebbc7208f.png)
Given the matrices $A$ and $e^{At}$ above, compute $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \big(e^{At}\big).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that 

$$
\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t} \big(e^{At}\big) = A \, e^{At}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At}) & =A\,{e}^{At} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & t{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & (t+1){e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
